prompt.context: Our client MJ Wineries produces wine in Sonoma Valley, California. MJ Wineries specializes in growing Chardonnay grapes and has won numerous awards for their famous full-bodied Chardonnay. Although MJ Wineries market share in Chardonnay remains strong, profitability has recently declined.
prompt.question: The CEO has hired your firm to recommend ways to immediately improve profitability.

clarifying_info.q: What is the current date / time context?
clarifying_info.a: It is currently January 1st, 2018; you can assume 2017 has just concluded.

clarifying_info.q: How long does it take to produce a bottle of wine?
clarifying_info.a: It takes at least nine months to produce a bottle of Chardonnay from the time the grapes are planted to the time the wine can be un-corked, but the wines get better as they age.

clarifying_info.q: Where does MJ Wineries grow its grapes / how large is the operation?
clarifying_info.a: MJ Wineries only produces wine in Sonoma Valley produced from grapes grown at one large 3,000 acre vineyard.

clarifying_info.q: Does MJ Wineries own its production equipment?
clarifying_info.a: Wine production is a very capital-intensive industry, but MJ Wineries owns the equipment they use to produce wines.

clarifying_info.q: How competitive is the wine market?
clarifying_info.a: There are some major wine producers but tens of thousands of small producers.

clarifying_info.q: Who are MJ Wineries' customers / distribution channels?
clarifying_info.a: Liquor stores are the primary distribution source; other channels include restaurants, bars/nightclubs, and supermarkets.

clarifying_info.q: What is the US market share by variety (in millions of dollars)?
clarifying_info.a: Chardonnay $2,500M; Cabernet Sauvignon $2,000M; Merlot $1,050M; Pinot Grigio $800M; Pinot Noir $300M; all other individual wine types are under $300M. Average profit margin on Chardonnay is 20%.

exhibits.title: Which wine do you consume the most? (US Adults)
exhibits.shows: A line chart (2007–2017) showing the percentage of US adults who consume white wine, red wine, and rosé wine the most.
exhibits.data: Y-axis: % of responses (0–70); three trend lines for White Wine, Red Wine, and Rosé Wine across years 2007–2017.

exhibits.title: Grape Variety Comparison Table
exhibits.shows: A table comparing seven grape varieties across wine type, key production locations, food pairing, consumption growth, and profit margin.
exhibits.data: Chardonnay: White, France/California, Fish & Chicken, 2% growth, 20% margin; Riesling: White, Germany/Eastern USA, Food friendly, 10% growth, 15% margin; Sauvignon Blanc: White, New Zealand/France, Seafood, 4% growth, 10% margin; Syrah: Red, Australia/France, Red meat, 2% growth, 18% margin; Merlot: Red, France/California, Red meat, 12% growth, 8% margin; Cabernet Sauvignon: Red, France/California, Red meat, 1% growth, 10% margin; Pinot Noir: Red, France/California, Food friendly, 12% growth, 15% margin.

framework: Revenue drivers: price changes, volume/quantity changes, mix/channel shifts
Cost drivers: fixed cost increases (new land, new equipment, marketing) and variable/input cost increases
Market-level factors: new entrants taking share, evolving customer tastes, Chardonnay losing popularity, other regions gaining prestige
Company-level factors: managerial capability, brand recognition, lack of product diversification, financing/cost of capital

questions.prompt: What could be impacting profitability at MJ Wineries? (Question 1 — framework / issue tree)
questions.guidance: A strong answer structures the problem as Profitability = Revenue − Costs, then drills into both sides. Revenue decreases: price cuts (coupons, competitive pressure), quantity decreases (new customers going elsewhere, channel issues), mix shift. Cost increases: fixed costs (new land, new equipment, marketing spend), variable/input price increases. Market factors: new entrants, evolving customer tastes (Chardonnay losing share), wine losing share to other spirits, other regions eroding California's prestige. Company factors: managerial capability, brand recognition decline, lack of diversification. Note: interviewer emphasises brainstorming and qualitative analysis — steer away from unnecessary calculations.

questions.prompt: Which grape variety should MJ Wineries consider for producing its new wine? (Question 2 — exhibit analysis)
questions.guidance: Hand Exhibit 1 and Exhibit 2. Candidate should identify that consumer preference is shifting from white wine to red wine (Exhibit 1). Among red wine varieties (Exhibit 2), Pinot Noir is the best recommendation because: (1) red wine is a growing consumer preference; (2) Merlot has strong consumption growth (~12%) but Pinot Noir also has 12% growth with higher margin (15% vs 8%); (3) Sonoma Valley is known for Pinot Noir production — climate and soil are suitable; (4) Pinot Noir is food-friendly, broadening marketing appeal. Candidates may justify other choices but should be guided toward Pinot Noir.

questions.prompt: What are some pros and cons for MJ Wineries to consider when moving into the Pinot Noir market? (Question 3)
questions.guidance: Pros: Pinot Noir is very popular and fast-growing in America; often sells at a higher price point than Chardonnay; product diversification insulates against consumer preference shifts; growing multiple varieties provides weather/crop-failure hedge; Pinot Noir is often produced alongside Chardonnay, which can elevate brand image. Cons: Pinot Noir is a red wine — not grown or produced the same way as Chardonnay; increased capital costs for red wine production; different and potentially harder competitive set; long lead time between planting and selling means it takes time to build a track record.

questions.prompt: What are some other ways MJ Wineries could increase revenue without introducing a new type of wine? (Question 4 — brainstorm contingency)
questions.guidance: See brainstorming section below. Look for creative, diverse ideas across product, experience, asset monetisation, and partnership categories. Award extra credit for structured buckets and novel but feasible ideas.

brainstorming.prompt: What are some other ways MJ Wineries could increase revenue without introducing a new type of wine?

categories.name: Other alcoholic products
ideas: Produce whiskey or spirits using existing land and facilities

categories.name: Winery experiences & events
ideas: Host weddings, corporate events, or private dinners at the winery
Offer hot air balloon rides over scenic Sonoma Valley

categories.name: Asset monetisation
ideas: Sell off a portion of the vineyard land to another winery or developer
Produce wine for small-batch producers using excess production capacity
Turn old wine barrels into high-end furniture (bars, coffee tables) sold via premium retailers

categories.name: Alternative agriculture
ideas: Use portions of the land to grow alternative high-value crops such as avocados or mushrooms

categories.name: Wine premium & aging
ideas: Age wines longer to sell higher-priced vintage Chardonnays at a premium price point

categories.name: Technology & yield
ideas: Invest in new agricultural technology to increase grape yield — produce more wine or sell excess grapes to other producers

categories.name: Education & hospitality
ideas: Turn part of the winery into a school or programme for aspiring wine producers

categories.name: Brand & marketing partnerships
ideas: Partner with renowned wine critics (e.g. Robert Parker) or major wine magazines to raise prestige and pricing power of existing Chardonnay

recommendation: MJ Wineries should expand into producing Pinot Noir
This will allow them to capture a greater share of the overall and growing red wine market
It will also help them diversify risk in case Chardonnay becomes less popular or the Chardonnay grape crop fails
risks: Wine consumer tastes are fickle — Pinot Noir growth may not be sustained
The craft brewing movement may shift consumer preferences toward beer, making further wine investment less attractive
Expanding into a new variety increases operational complexity and capital requirements
next_steps: Begin developing capabilities for producing Pinot Noir and plant new grape vines
Purchase additional equipment required for red wine production
Explore contingency revenue levers (events, partnerships, aging premium) in parallel to reduce reliance on a single product line
